summaries.example: Imagine you test several pieces of a yellow metal. Each piece is heavy, bends, and melts in a certain way. You may reasonably expect the next piece to behave similarly. But unless you know what is happening inside the metal, you cannot be completely certain. Locke says this is much like our knowledge of nature: careful experience gives us real, useful knowledge, but not perfect certainty.
summaries.summary: Locke’s philosophy of science asks what humans can know about nature. Older thinkers often pictured science as certain knowledge proved from necessary truths. Locke kept that high ideal, but he also saw that experiments and senses are the best tools available to people studying natural things. We can observe that qualities regularly occur together—for example, that a certain metal is yellow, heavy, bendable, and meltable. Yet we usually cannot see the hidden structure that causes these qualities, or prove that they must always occur together. Locke therefore calls our natural knowledge sensitive knowledge. It is more than a guess because it rests on experience, but it is less than perfect certainty. Locke also discusses the corpuscular hypothesis, according to which bodies are built from tiny parts. He often uses this idea to explain how qualities might arise, while also noting puzzles about sensation, motion, gravity, and how tiny parts stick together. Because of this tension, scholars disagree about exactly how strongly Locke accepted the hypothesis. His connection with Newton raises another question: whether new mathematical and experimental science could make natural philosophy more certain. The entry presents these questions without treating them as settled.
key_ideas: Locke admired experiments because they help us learn from observation instead of relying only on speculation.
He thought perfect scientific certainty about natural things would require knowing their hidden essences and necessary connections.
Human beings usually know nature through sensitive knowledge: repeated observations, tests, and reasonable expectations.
Locke sometimes spoke as if the corpuscular hypothesis were true, but he also pointed out serious problems it could not clearly explain.
The source describes scholarly disagreement about whether Locke accepted this hypothesis, rejected it, or used it mainly as a helpful model.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us understand why science can be both powerful and limited. Observations and experiments can give us dependable knowledge, even when we cannot see every cause. It also teaches an important lesson about scientific models: a model may organize evidence and suggest explanations while still leaving difficult questions unanswered. Locke’s ideas invite us to separate what we observe from what we think explains it.

important_terms.definition: The study of how we know things, including what counts as evidence and how certain knowledge can be.
Knowledge that is certain and universal, like a carefully proven fact in geometry.
Knowledge based on what our senses repeatedly show us. It can be well supported without being completely certain.
The hidden inside structure of a thing that makes it the kind of thing it is.
The group of visible or other known qualities that we use to name and sort a thing.
The idea that visible things are made from very tiny parts whose size, shape, number, and motion help explain what we observe.

questions_to_think_about: Can repeated tests make a belief very trustworthy without making it absolutely certain?
What might be hidden inside an object that our senses cannot detect?
Why might a model be useful even if we are not sure it is completely true?

summaries.example: Suppose a researcher finds that a substance has a particular color, mass, flexibility, and melting behavior in every tested sample. Locke would allow a carefully formed idea of the substance based on qualities found to coexist in experience. But this does not reveal the substance’s real essence, nor does it show by necessity that every future sample will display the same combination. A theory about microscopic particles might explain the pattern, yet Locke asks whether the theory can actually account for the connection between particle motion and the resulting sensory qualities.
summaries.summary: The entry examines Locke’s attempt to develop an account of natural knowledge suited to experimental science. The inherited ideal of scientia required certainty, universality, knowledge of causes, and demonstration from secure premises. In natural philosophy, that would mean knowing the real essences of material substances and deducing the necessary connections between those essences and the substances’ qualities or powers. Locke argues that humans cannot generally achieve this. Our senses are not fine enough to reveal the minute constitution of bodies, and we lack access to the extensive causal network in which bodies may stand. Nor can we ordinarily discover a necessary connection between a substance’s observable qualities. We therefore rely on trials, observation, and induction. This produces sensitive knowledge: genuine, experience-grounded knowledge of effects and coexisting qualities, but not the certainty of scientia. The entry then analyzes a tension in Locke’s treatment of the corpuscular hypothesis. He often speaks as if bodies are composed of tiny particles and as if observable qualities depend on their primary qualities. Yet he also calls the theory a hypothesis and identifies serious explanatory difficulties. It is unclear how particle motion could produce sensations, how motion is communicated by impact, or how particles cohere into bodies; Newtonian gravity also challenges strict contact action. Scholars consequently disagree about whether Locke accepts the theory, rejects it, or uses it as a provisional framework constrained by deeper epistemological and metaphysical limits. The final section compares Locke with Newton in method, knowledge, space, body, mind, and gravity.
key_ideas: Locke contrasts the Aristotelian ideal of scientia—certain knowledge of necessary truths and causes—with the evidence-based knowledge available in experimental natural philosophy.
Scientific knowledge of a material substance would require knowing its real essence and the necessary connections by which its qualities and powers follow from that essence.
Human observers generally encounter effects and regular co-occurrences, not necessary connections. Induction can therefore yield probability rather than demonstrative certainty.

The corpuscular hypothesis appears in Locke’s explanations of primary, secondary, and tertiary qualities, yet Locke also stresses its inability to make sensation, motion, cohesion, and possibly gravity intelligible.
The entry presents competing interpretations: Locke may have accepted corpuscularianism, remained agnostic about it, or used it strategically while emphasizing its limits.
Locke and Newton share an emphasis on the limits of human access to inner constitutions, but the entry leaves open how far Locke adopted Newton’s mathematical methodology.
summaries.why_it_matters: Locke’s analysis clarifies a central issue in science: the difference between observing regular patterns and knowing why those patterns must occur. It also shows how theories can be influential without yielding complete understanding. His discussion anticipates later concerns about induction, unobservable entities, reduction, and the relation between physical explanation and metaphysical assumptions. The debate over his corpuscularianism further demonstrates why interpreting a philosopher requires attending to tensions across an entire work rather than isolating a few apparently decisive passages.

important_terms.definition: Locke’s account of knowing: knowledge involves perceiving agreement or disagreement among ideas.
Certain, universal knowledge, traditionally associated with necessary truths, causes, and demonstration.
Immediate certainty in which the mind grasps a connection without intermediate reasoning.
Certain knowledge reached through intermediate steps, such as a proof.
A less-than-certain but genuine kind of knowledge about experienced effects and regularly coexisting qualities.
The internal constitution that makes a thing what it is and grounds its observable qualities; for Locke, it is generally unknown.
The observable-quality complex used to classify and name a thing.
A theory that bodies consist of minute particles, commonly emphasizing their size, shape, number, and motion and sometimes reducing observable qualities to them.

questions_to_think_about: Is a theory genuinely explanatory if it describes hidden particles but cannot show how their motions produce sensations such as color or sound?
Does regular coexistence of qualities justify a general expectation, or only make it probable?
Can Locke consistently treat the corpuscular hypothesis as both a useful account and a theory whose explanatory resources are inadequate?
Would Newton’s mathematical physics move natural philosophy closer to scientia, or only strengthen sensitive knowledge?
What is the difference between a physical theory and a more basic metaphysical claim about what a thing is?

summaries.example: You notice that whenever your school’s metal water bottle is dropped, it makes a loud sound. You can form a reasonable expectation that the next drop will also make a sound. But you may not know the bottle’s tiny internal structure or exactly how moving parts produce the sound you hear. For Locke, experience supports the expectation, yet it does not turn it into a necessary truth like a result proved in geometry.
summaries.summary: Locke’s philosophy of science focuses on a basic problem: how can people learn about a natural world whose deepest workings they cannot directly see? He inherited an older ideal called scientia. On this ideal, genuine science gives certain and universal knowledge of necessary truths and their causes, much as geometry gives knowledge through proof. Locke respected that ideal, but he thought it was too demanding for human study of material nature. To reach it, we would need to know the real essence of each substance—the hidden structure that makes it what it is—and the necessary connections that make its qualities follow from that structure. Our senses usually reveal only effects and observable properties. We can find that certain qualities regularly occur together and can use experiments to make reasonable predictions. Locke calls this sensitive knowledge. It is better than an unsupported guess because it is grounded in experience, but it does not guarantee that the same pattern must occur in every unobserved case. Locke often discusses the corpuscular hypothesis, which explains bodies as made from tiny material parts. Their size, shape, number, and motion are supposed to help explain the qualities we observe. However, Locke also points to major difficulties. It is hard to understand how motion could produce color, taste, or sound; how motion passes from one body to another; and how tiny parts hold together to form larger bodies. Gravity raises a further question about whether all action requires contact. Because Locke both uses the hypothesis and stresses its limits, scholars disagree about his exact position. The entry also considers how his views compare with Newton’s developing mathematical physics.
key_ideas: Locke compares two pictures of science: one seeks certainty through proof, while the newer experimental approach learns from observations and tests.
He thinks people cannot usually discover the hidden structures and necessary causes needed for perfect science about nature.
Sensitive knowledge is not mere opinion. It is based on qualities that experience shows occurring together, although predictions beyond observed cases remain probable.
Locke connects several of his ideas about substances with the corpuscular hypothesis, but he also questions whether that theory can explain everything it promises.
The theory faces puzzles about how particles create sensations, pass on motion, stick together, and perhaps attract one another across distance.
Scholars interpret Locke differently: some emphasize his apparent support for corpuscles, while others emphasize his caution and skepticism.
summaries.why_it_matters: This subject matters because it teaches us to ask what evidence can really show. A successful experiment may reveal a dependable pattern without revealing its ultimate cause. Locke also helps us see that scientific theories have both strengths and limits: they can organize observations, guide research, and suggest explanations while leaving deeper questions open. These are still useful habits for evaluating claims about things we cannot directly observe.

important_terms.definition: The study of knowledge: how we get it, what supports it, and how certain it is.
A very strong ideal of knowledge: certain truths that can be demonstrated and apply universally.
Knowledge based on repeated sensory experience and observation. It is real knowledge, though usually not certain in the strongest sense.
The hidden internal structure that makes a substance what it is and helps explain its qualities.
The set of qualities we notice and use to classify something, such as a metal’s color and weight.
A theory that explains ordinary objects as collections of extremely small material parts.
A quality that belongs to a body’s parts, such as size, shape, number, or motion, in the theory Locke discusses.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a pattern observed many times still fall short of certainty?
Would seeing smaller parts of an object automatically explain why it has its larger-scale qualities?
Can a scientific hypothesis be useful even when it has serious unanswered problems?
Why would gravity create difficulty for a theory that says bodies interact only by touching?
How is a hidden cause different from an observable quality?
